Estimating and validating treatment effects for survival outcomes

Vignette 2 of 4

November 14, 2026

Source: vignettes/Survival-examples.Rmd
Survival-examples.Rmd

This vignette demonstrates how to use precmed to estimate average and conditional average treatment effects (ATEs and CATEs) for survival outcomes. Using fully synthetic data inspired by a multiple sclerosis treatment comparison, we model restricted mean time lost, compare CATE scoring methods through internal validation, and interpret treatment effects in responder subgroups.

Load required packages 

library(precmed)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

Example data

We generate fully synthetic data with simulate_survival(). Its treatment and outcome models are illustrative and do not use patient records or represent clinical estimates. The default event model simulates greater drug 1 benefit at older ages and with more previous relapses. These illustrative interactions preserve the direction of associations in the package’s original survival example but are much weaker; they should not be interpreted as clinical estimates. We generate 4,000 patients and set a seed for reproducibility. The propensity model assigns treatment, so the group sizes vary with the simulated data. Its default intercept targets approximately 54% receiving drug 1, similar to the aggregate treatment split in the package’s original 4,000-patient survival example; individual records are not used. The result contains nine variables: six baseline characteristics, treatment, observed time and an event indicator.

survival_data <- simulate_survival(n = 4000, seed = 20261114)

Treatment is assigned according to the propensity model; its weights can be changed to explore different treatment proportions and degrees of overlap. For example, simulate_survival(n = 4000, seed = 1, ps_weights = c(intercept = -1), conditional_hr = 0.8) changes the propensity intercept and the conditional HR at age 48. Named ps_weights and lp_weights override the specified defaults; see ?simulate_survival for their definitions. The table below summarizes baseline characteristics by treatment group.

The treatment and survival outcome variables have distinct roles:

  • We will use y as the survival outcome, which is the number of days until the first relapse or censoring, whichever comes first.

  • We will use d as the event indicator, where 11 represents an event and 00 represents censoring. The censoring rate is 63.3%.

  • We will use trt as the treatment variable, which has 2 drugs (drug0 and drug1).

For convenience, age is centered at 48 years and previous_cost is centered at 14,362 USD and divided by 24,266 USD. These transformations change the scale of the coefficients, not the information in the covariates.

Estimate the average treatment effect

Unadjusted treatment comparison

We first compare time to first relapse between treatment groups using a Cox model with treatment as the only predictor. This unadjusted, marginal association does not account for differences in patient characteristics.

library(survival)
output_cox <- coxph(Surv(y, d) ~ trt, data = survival_data)
summary(output_cox)
#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(y, d) ~ trt, data = survival_data)
#> 
#>   n= 4000, number of events= 1466 
#> 
#>              coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)    
#> trtdrug1 -0.40665   0.66588  0.05243 -7.756 8.78e-15 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>          exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> trtdrug1    0.6659      1.502    0.6008    0.7379
#> 
#> Concordance= 0.547  (se = 0.007 )
#> Likelihood ratio test= 60.34  on 1 df,   p=8e-15
#> Wald test            = 60.15  on 1 df,   p=9e-15
#> Score (logrank) test = 60.98  on 1 df,   p=6e-15

The estimated hazard ratio (HR) for drug 1 versus drug 0 is 0.67. It compares instantaneous relapse hazards among patients still event-free and does not by itself establish a causal treatment effect.

We can examine the proportional-hazards assumption using scaled Schoenfeld residuals. A roughly horizontal curve is consistent with a constant HR over time; the dashed curves show approximate 95% uncertainty bands.

ph_unadjusted <- cox.zph(output_cox, transform = "identity")
print(ph_unadjusted)
#>        chisq df    p
#> trt     1.52  1 0.22
#> GLOBAL  1.52  1 0.22
plot(ph_unadjusted, var = "trt", hr = TRUE, resid = FALSE,
     xlab = "Days since treatment initiation",
     ylab = "Unadjusted hazard ratio: drug1 vs drug0")
abline(h = exp(coef(output_cox)[1]), lty = 3, col = "steelblue")

The dotted line is the constant HR from the Cox model. The smooth curve suggests how the treatment association may vary over time; it is a diagnostic rather than a precise estimate at every time point. The proportional-hazards test for the treatment term gives p = 0.217. This test assesses whether the treatment association changes over time; a large p-value does not prove that the HR is constant. Later follow-up is less informative when fewer patients remain at risk, as reflected in the wider uncertainty bands.

Covariate-adjusted treatment comparison

Next, we adjust for age, sex, previous medical cost and previous relapses using a Cox model:

output_cox_adjusted <- coxph(
  Surv(y, d) ~ trt + age + female + previous_cost + previous_number_relapses,
  data = survival_data
)
summary(output_cox_adjusted)
#> Call:
#> coxph(formula = Surv(y, d) ~ trt + age + female + previous_cost + 
#>     previous_number_relapses, data = survival_data)
#> 
#>   n= 4000, number of events= 1466 
#> 
#>                               coef exp(coef)  se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)    
#> trtdrug1                 -0.438415  0.645058  0.053296 -8.226  < 2e-16 ***
#> age                       0.007923  1.007954  0.002987  2.652  0.00800 ** 
#> female                    0.137659  1.147584  0.058880  2.338  0.01939 *  
#> previous_cost             0.168180  1.183150  0.061517  2.734  0.00626 ** 
#> previous_number_relapses  0.073957  1.076761  0.029035  2.547  0.01086 *  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>                          exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> trtdrug1                    0.6451     1.5502    0.5811    0.7161
#> age                         1.0080     0.9921    1.0021    1.0139
#> female                      1.1476     0.8714    1.0225    1.2880
#> previous_cost               1.1831     0.8452    1.0488    1.3348
#> previous_number_relapses    1.0768     0.9287    1.0172    1.1398
#> 
#> Concordance= 0.565  (se = 0.009 )
#> Likelihood ratio test= 85.61  on 5 df,   p=<2e-16
#> Wald test            = 85.2  on 5 df,   p=<2e-16
#> Score (logrank) test = 86.09  on 5 df,   p=<2e-16

The adjusted HR is 0.65, compared with 0.67 in the unadjusted model. The treatment groups have substantial overlap in age in this synthetic example; model adjustment and appropriate assumptions still matter. An adjusted HR is conditional on the included covariates and is not automatically a causal average treatment effect.

ph_adjusted <- cox.zph(output_cox_adjusted, transform = "identity")
print(ph_adjusted)
#>                           chisq df     p
#> trt                      2.2505  1 0.134
#> age                      2.7471  1 0.097
#> female                   0.4168  1 0.519
#> previous_cost            0.1446  1 0.704
#> previous_number_relapses 0.0283  1 0.866
#> GLOBAL                   4.6952  5 0.454
plot(ph_adjusted, var = "trt", hr = TRUE, resid = FALSE,
     xlab = "Days since treatment initiation",
     ylab = "Adjusted hazard ratio: drug1 vs drug0")
abline(h = exp(coef(output_cox_adjusted)["trtdrug1"]), lty = 3, col = "steelblue")

For the adjusted model, the proportional-hazards test for the treatment term gives p = 0.134. This test assesses whether the treatment HR changes over time; it is not a test of whether the treatment effect is zero. A large p-value does not establish that the HR is constant. The global proportional-hazards test gives p = 0.454 and assesses the model covariates jointly, so evidence of non-proportional hazards may arise from covariates other than treatment.

Population-level treatment comparison over a fixed horizon

The unadjusted Cox model compares treatment groups without accounting for differences in their characteristics. The adjusted Cox model accounts for the selected covariates, but its HR is conditional on those covariates and summarizes the treatment association using a single HR. The diagnostics can be used to assess changes in this association over time; estimates often become less informative later in follow-up. Neither comparison directly describes the average time patients remain relapse-free under each treatment.

We now use atefit() to estimate population-level outcomes over a specified follow-up horizon. For restricted mean survival time (RMST) and restricted mean time lost (RMTL), it combines outcome and propensity score models with an adjustment for censoring to estimate population-level outcomes under each treatment. These measures summarize time over the chosen period without requiring a constant treatment HR. Under appropriate assumptions, the population-level comparison can be interpreted as a causal treatment effect. atefit() also estimates a population-level cumulative hazard ratio at the horizon. It uses bootstrap resampling to estimate uncertainty for all reported measures.

RMST is the average event-free time up to a chosen horizon, tau0; RMTL is tau0 - RMST. The RMTL ratio compares time lost under drug 1 with time lost under drug 0 over that horizon; for relapse, a ratio below 1 favors drug 1. Its interpretation depends on the horizon. Chapter 20 discusses RMTL for ratio-based treatment effects (Jiang et al. 2026).

The cumulative hazard ratio compares the cumulative hazards, −log⁡(S(tau0))-\log(S(tau0)), under the two treatments. atefit() estimates the treatment-specific survival probabilities using augmented inverse probability of treatment weighting (AIPTW), combining outcome, propensity score and censoring models without discretizing event times. The estimator requires appropriate censoring assumptions and a correctly specified censoring model; its treatment-model double robustness does not protect against censoring-model misspecification. The calculation reuses the treatment-specific Cox outcome fits, propensity scores and censoring model used for RMST. This ratio is distinct from an instantaneous HR. If either estimated survival probability is outside the interval (0, 1), the ratio is undefined; bootstrap inference is also unavailable if any replicate is undefined.

For this example, we choose an illustrative horizon: the smaller 95th percentile of observed follow-up in the two treatment groups.

tau0 <- with(survival_data,
             min(quantile(y[trt == "drug1"], 0.95), quantile(y[trt == "drug0"], 0.95)))
tau0
#> [1] 765.4456

The horizon is approximately 765.4 days. It defines the period over which we will compare restricted mean outcomes. This choice is not derived from the proportional-hazards diagnostics and does not establish that the HR is constant before the horizon. It uses observed times, including censoring, and does not guarantee sufficient follow-up; inspect numbers at risk and censoring near the horizon in both groups and choose a clinically meaningful horizon with adequate support.

The RMTL estimator is doubly robust with respect to the propensity score (PS) and outcome models: under the required assumptions, either model may be correctly specified. It also depends on inverse probability of censoring weights (IPCW) and a correctly specified censoring model. The function provides standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values based on bootstrap. If an out-of-range RMST estimate is replaced by an outcome-model estimate, that fallback does not retain the doubly robust guarantee.

IPCW adjusts for censoring by weighting patients according to their estimated probability of remaining uncensored. Causal interpretation requires assumptions including no unmeasured treatment confounding, adequate treatment overlap, appropriate censoring assumptions and sufficient follow-up. Chapter 17 discusses identification of treatment effects in non-randomized data (Hoogland et al. 2026). The Cox HR and the RMTL ratio describe different aspects of survival and should be interpreted separately.

The mandatory arguments for atefit() are:

  • The response argument specifies the type of outcome in the data. For survival outcomes, response = “survival”. This informs the function of the necessary arguments and methods to use.

  • The argument data indicates the data frame in which the outcome, treatment and covariates specified in either cate.model or ps.model should be fetched.

  • The argument cate.model specifies the CATE model as a formula, with the survival object from the survival package, Surv(y, d), supplied on the left-hand side and the explanatory covariates supplied on the right-hand side. In the example below, we chose to specify to CATE as a linear combination of the following covariates: age, sex, medical costs in the year prior to treatment initiation, and number of relapses in the year prior to treatment initiation. Non-linear or interaction terms could also be included. Note that the treatment variable is not supplied in cate.model since this is an outcome model.

  • The ps.model argument specifies the PS model as a formula, with the treatment variable trt on the left-hand side and the covariates (age and previous treatment in this example) on the right-hand side. The variable trt must be supplied as a numeric variable taking only 2 values, “1” for active treatment and “0” for control or comparator. If it is not the case, atefit() will stop with error if trt takes more than 2 distinct values or will automatically transform trt into a numeric variable. In this example, trt (a factor variable taking values “drug0” and “drug1”) was transformed and a warning message was left to the user (see output below): Variable trt was recoded to 0/1 with drug0->0 and drug1->1. If the data are from a RCT, it suffices to specify ps.model = trt ~ 1. The PS model is used in the doubly robust RMTL estimation.

We also specify the optional argument tau0, the horizon for RMST and RMTL, using the value calculated above.

Now estimate the ATE using an outcome model with age, sex, previous cost and previous relapses, and a PS model with age and previous_treatment.

output_atefit <- atefit(response = "survival",
                        data = survival_data,
                        cate.model = survival::Surv(y, d) ~ age + female + previous_cost + previous_number_relapses,
                        ps.model = trt ~ age + previous_treatment,
                        tau0 = tau0,
                        seed = 999)
#> Warning in data.preproc.surv(fun = "drinf", cate.model = cate.model, ps.model = ps.model, : Variable trt was recoded to 0/1 with drug0->0 and drug1->1.

When verbose = 1, the function outputs a progress bar in the console.

output_atefit
#> Average treatment effect:
#> 
#>                               estimate         SE   CI.lower   CI.upper
#> log.rmtl.ratio              -0.3129050 0.04510642 -0.4013120 -0.2244980
#> log.cumulative.hazard.ratio -0.5504311 0.09158371 -0.7299318 -0.3709303
#>                                   pvalue
#> log.rmtl.ratio              4.004019e-12
#> log.cumulative.hazard.ratio 1.853611e-09
#> 
#> Estimated RMST:
#> 
#>       estimate       SE CI.lower CI.upper pvalue
#> rmst1 514.0616 7.961516 498.4573 529.6658      0
#> rmst0 421.7052 9.071721 403.9249 439.4854      0
#> Warning in print.atefit(x): Variable trt was recoded to 0/1 with drug0->0 and drug1->1.

The output of atefit() shows the point estimate, standard error (“SE”), lower (“CI.lower”) and upper (“CI.upper”) bound of the 95% confidence interval, and the p-value (“pvalue”) for 4 estimands:

  • the restricted mean survival time under drug 1 ($rmst1)

  • the restricted mean survival time under drug 0 ($rmst0)

  • the log RMTL ratio ($log.rmtl.ratio), which is the log of the ratio of tau0 - $rmst1 divided by tau0 - $rmst0

  • the log population-level cumulative hazard ratio at tau0 ($log.cumulative.hazard.ratio).

The following comparison places the earlier Cox models alongside a covariate-adjusted Cox model censored at tau0 and the population-level cumulative hazard ratio. The first three rows are instantaneous Cox HRs with model-based confidence intervals; the last is a ratio of cumulative hazards with a bootstrap-based confidence interval.

Comparison Ratio 95% CI
Unadjusted Cox, all follow-up 0.67 0.60 to 0.74
Adjusted Cox, all follow-up 0.65 0.58 to 0.72
Adjusted Cox, through tau0 0.65 0.58 to 0.72
AIPTW cumulative hazard ratio at tau0 0.58 0.48 to 0.69

The differences reflect covariate adjustment, the follow-up horizon and the estimand and estimation method. In particular, the cumulative hazard ratio is not an instantaneous Cox HR; similarity or differences between the numbers alone do not establish which model is correct.

For example, the log RMTL ratio of -0.31 and the 95% confidence interval of (-0.4, -0.22) are displayed in the output. The estimated ratio and its interval can be obtained by exponentiating these log-scale values. A ratio above 1 indicates more time lost before tau0 under drug 1; the interval describes uncertainty in that comparison. The RMST estimates provide the corresponding event-free times up to tau0.

The output of atefit() is expressed in terms of treatment 0 vs 1, where the RMTL and cumulative hazard ratios are expressed as the ratio of the treatment coded as 1 over the treatment coded as 0. If the treatment variable is not coded as 0/1 in the data set, the function returns a warning output_atefit$warning which indicates what key was used to recode the treatment variable into a 0/1 variable.

output_atefit$warning
#> [1] "Variable trt was recoded to 0/1 with drug0->0 and drug1->1.\n"

Using plot(output_atefit), a histograms is generated of the point estimates across the n.boot bootstrap iterations for 4 estimands (rmst1, rmst0, log.rmtl.ratio, log.cumulative.hazard.ratio). A red vertical line marks the estimate from the original sample.

plot(output_atefit)

Histograms of bootstrap estimates for the four reported quantities.

Estimate CATE scores

Chapter 17 describes treatment effect heterogeneity and CATE prediction (Hoogland et al. 2026). In this example, scores are on the log-RMTL-ratio scale, so exponentiating a score gives an estimated conditional RMTL ratio. Lower scores indicate greater estimated benefit from drug 1. Fitting scores on the full dataset does not establish their performance in new patients.

Now we have calculated the ATE we know the effect of both treatments on average, but this effect might not be the same for all patients. Thus, it might be worthwhile to check if there are subgroups that respond differently to the treatments. We can calculate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) score which calculates the ATE for different subgroups in the data. If no internal validation is needed (we get back to that later), we can use the catefit() function to a model directly to the entire data set to estimate the CATE score. For the catefit() function we have to define the score.method. This arguments specifies the precision medicine (PM) method to be used to calculate the CATE scores. There are a total of 5 scoring methods implemented:

The mandatory arguments in catefit() are:

  • response: “survival” in this example because we use have data with a survival outcome (e.g., number of days until the first relapse or censoring))

  • data: the name of the data set. (survival_data)

  • score.method: argument specifies the precision medicine (PM) methods to be used to calculate the CATE scores. There are a total of 5 scoring methods implemented:

    • poisson fits a Poisson model separately by treatment group.

    • boosting uses gradient boosted regression models (GBM) separately by treatment group.

    • randomForest fits a random forest model by treatment group.

    • twoReg implements the doubly robust two regressions estimator in (Yadlowsky et al. 2021).

    • contrastReg implements the doubly robust contrast regression estimator from (Yadlowsky et al. 2021).

  • cate.model: A formula describing the outcome model to be fitted. The outcome must appear on the left-hand side. In the example, we choose to specify to outcome model as a linear combination of the following covariates: age, sex, medical costs in the year prior to treatment initiation, and number of relapses in the year prior to treatment initiation. Non-linear or interaction terms could also be included. Note that the treatment variable is not supplied in cate.model since this is an outcome model.

  • ps.model: A formula describing the propensity score (PS) model to be fitted. The treatment must appear on the left-hand side and the covariates (age and previous treatment in this example) on the right-hand side. The variable trt must be supplied as a numeric variable taking only 2 values, 1 for active treatment and 0 for control or comparator. If it is not the case, the function will stop with error if trt takes more than 2 distinct values or will automatically transform trt into a numeric variable. In this example, trt (a factor variable taking values “drug0” and “drug1”) was transformed and a warning message was left to the user (see output below): Variable trt was recoded to 0/1 with drug0->0 and drug1->1. If the data are from a RCT, it suffices to specify ps.model = trt ~ 1. Note that the PS model is only used in the estimation of the 2 doubly robust methods (two and contrast regressions).

We also specified the following non-mandatory arguments to fit with the data and problem at hand: initial.predictor.method, tau0, higher.y, seed, and plot.gbmperf.

  • initial.predictor.method specifies how predictions of the outcome are estimated in two regressions and contrast regression. Flexible models can be used such as GBM (“boosting”), random forests (“randomForest”) or logistic regression (“logistic”). We chose “logistic” because it is relatively faster than boosting methods and random forest.

  • tau0 is the horizon for RMTL, chosen as described above; assess follow-up support near this horizon in both treatment groups.

  • higher.y was set to TRUE because relapse is a negative event and longer time to first relapse is more desirable in our example. Hence, we are telling the function that subgroups of high responders to drug1 vs drug0 should have later onset of the first relapse. For a positive event such as discharge, a shorter time may instead be preferable, so higher.y = FALSE may be appropriate. It is important for this argument to match with the nature of y outcome because it will affect how the subgroups are defined by the CATE scores and the performance metrics.

  • We set a random seed seed = 999 to reproduce the results.

  • We avoided generating the boosting performance plots by specifying plot.gbmperf = FALSE.

Please see the Function description section for details.

If you run into errors or warnings with your data, it might be helpful to go over the descriptions to see if you need to alter the default values. In this toy example, we keep the default values of the remaining arguments. For this toy example we selected randomForest and contrastReg to limit run time.

tau0 <- with(survival_data,
             min(quantile(y[trt == "drug1"], 0.95), quantile(y[trt == "drug0"], 0.95)))

output_catefit <- catefit(response = "survival",
                          data = survival_data,
                          score.method = c( "randomForest", "contrastReg"),
                          cate.model = survival::Surv(y, d) ~ age + female + previous_cost + previous_number_relapses,
                          ps.model = trt ~ age + previous_treatment,
                          initial.predictor.method = "logistic",
                          tau0 = tau0, 
                          higher.y = TRUE,
                          seed = 999,
                          plot.gbmperf = FALSE)
#> Warning in data.preproc.surv(fun = "catefit", cate.model = cate.model, ps.model = ps.model, : Variable trt was recoded to 0/1 with drug0->0 and drug1->1.

Each method specified in score.method has the following sets of results in catefit():

  1. score contains the log-transformed estimated CATE scores for each subject. The relationship between covariates and the score depends on the scoring method. For survival outcomes, lower scores correspond to high responders to drug 1 when higher.y = TRUE; higher scores correspond to high responders when higher.y = FALSE. In our example, the survival outcome is time to first relapse, which is a negative event, so higher values indicate later onset of the first relapse. Hence, we specify higher.y = TRUE in the example. Each subject has 1 CATE score so the length of this output is 4,000 for our toy example. Below we show the CATE scores estimated with contrast regression for the first 6 subjects in the data.
length(output_catefit$score.contrastReg)
#> [1] 4000
head(output_catefit$score.contrastReg)
#> [1] -0.2745338  0.1813588 -0.4858946 -0.1780494 -0.2154102 -0.2017210
  1. coefficients contains the estimated coefficients of the CATE score for each scoring method. It is a data frame of the covariates (including intercept) as rows and scoring methods as columns. In our toy example, there are 4 covariates in the cate.model, plus the intercept, so there are 5 rows of estimated coefficients within each column. Boosting method does not estimate coefficients (it directly predicts the score) so they do not have coefficient results here.
output_catefit$coefficients
#>                           contrastReg
#> (Intercept)              -0.236152165
#> age                      -0.027102807
#> female                    0.044128300
#> previous_cost            -0.008540983
#> previous_number_relapses -0.122342558

The contrast-regression coefficients above describe how the fitted log-RMTL score changes with each covariate. They are estimates from these synthetic data.

The chr outputs provide subgroup cumulative hazard ratios at tau0, estimated using the same outcome, propensity-score and censoring models as the subgroup RMTL estimates. The hr outputs are instead covariate-adjusted Cox hazard ratios, with follow-up censored at tau0. These are different measures and should be interpreted separately. An undefined cumulative hazard ratio is returned as NA, with a warning recorded for the subgroup. Use measure = "cumulative_hr" in survival validation plots and box plots to display cumulative hazard ratios.

  1. ate contains estimated ATEs by each nested subgroup of high responders to drug 1 defined by prop.cutoff. The subgroups are defined based on the estimated CATE scores with the specified scoring method. In this example, we show the estimated ATEs of subgroups identified by CATE scores of the contrast regression. For example, the estimated ATE for the subgroup of subjects constructed based on the 50% (“prop0.5”) lowest CATE scores estimated from the contrast regression is 0.6.
output_catefit$ate.contrastReg
#>   prop0.5   prop0.6   prop0.7   prop0.8   prop0.9     prop1 
#> 0.6020295 0.6054979 0.6340460 0.6701166 0.7011565 0.7313194

The corresponding subgroup cumulative hazard ratios are available as:

output_catefit$chr.contrastReg
#>   prop0.5   prop0.6   prop0.7   prop0.8   prop0.9     prop1 
#> 0.4122234 0.3910096 0.4437420 0.4706669 0.5303529 0.5767012

You are encouraged to summarize and visualize the outputs in whichever way that fits their particular situation outside the package’s functions. For example, it is possible to plot the densities of all CATE scores with ggplot. The score distributions summarize variation in predicted treatment benefit across patients.

dataplot <- data.frame(score = factor(rep(c("Random Forest", "Contrast regression"), 
                                          each = length(output_catefit$score.randomForest))), 
                       value = c(output_catefit$score.randomForest,output_catefit$score.contrastReg))

dataplot %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = score)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_classic() + 
  labs(x = "Estimated CATE score", y = "Density", fill = "Method")

The random forest produces a wider distribution of estimated CATE scores than contrast regression. This may reflect greater flexibility, estimation noise or overfitting; the narrower distribution could also reflect constraints imposed by the contrast-regression model. The plot alone cannot distinguish these explanations. The internal validation below assesses whether the predicted differences in treatment benefit persist in patients not used to fit the scores.

Internally validate CATE scores

How internal validation works

For broader guidance on validation strategies and the assessment of discrimination, calibration, and decision accuracy, see Chapter 19, “Validation of prediction models for patient outcomes and individualized treatment effect” (Thao et al. 2026).

In each iteration, scores are fitted in a training set and evaluated in a separate validation set. For example, the 60% of validation patients with the lowest scores form a high-responder subgroup in this example. Repeating the split shows variation across iterations. Selecting the best method using the same validation results can make its reported performance optimistic; an independent evaluation can assess the selected method.

The catecv() function provides the same estimation as the catefit() but via cross-validation (CV). With the catecv() function internal CV is applied to reduce optimism in choosing the CATE estimation method that captures the most treatment effect heterogeneity. The CV is applied by repeating the following steps cv.n times:

  • Split the data into a training and validation set according to train.prop argument. The training and validation sets must be balanced with respect to covariate distributions and doubly robust treatment effect estimates (see error.max argument).

  • Estimate the CATE score in the training set with the specified scoring method.

  • Predict the CATE score in the validation set using the scoring model fitted from the training set.

  • Build nested subgroups of treatment responders in the training and validation sets, separately, and estimate the ATE within each nested subgroup. For each element i of prop.cutoff argument (e.g., prop.cutoff[i] = 0.6), take the following steps:

    • Identify high responders as observations with the 60% (i.e., prop.cutoff[i]x100%) lowest (if higher.y = TRUE) or highest (if higher.y = FALSE) estimated CATE scores.

    • Estimate the ATE in the subgroup of high responders using a doubly robust estimator.

    • Conversely, identify low responders as observations with the 40% (i.e., 1 - prop.cutoff[i]x100%) highest (if higher.y = TRUE) or lowest (if higher.y = FALSE) estimated CATE scores.

    • Estimate the ATE in the subgroup of low responders using a doubly robust estimator.

  • If abc = TRUE, calculate the area between the ATE and the series of ATEs in nested subgroups of high responders in the validation set. (for more information about the abc score, see Validation curves and the ABC statistics)

  • Build mutually exclusive subgroups of treatment responders in the training and validation sets, separately, and estimate the ATE within each subgroup. Mutually exclusive subgroups are built by splitting the estimated CATE scores according to prop.multi.

Run internal validation

For each scoring method, catecv() also returns chr.<method> matrices for nested and disjoint subgroups in the training and validation folds. overall.chr.train and overall.chr.valid report the corresponding overall fold estimates.

Now we can use the catecv() function to run internal validation to compare the different scoring methods. The mandatory arguments are similar to atefit() and catefit(): The mandatory arguments are: response, data, score.method, cate.model, and ps.model. See above for more details on these arguments. For this toy example we again selected randomForest and contrastReg limit run time.

We also specified the following non-mandatory arguments to fit with the data and problem at hand: initial.predictor.method, ipcw.model, verbose, followup.time, tau0, higher.y, cv.n, surv.min, seed, and plot.gbmperf.

  • initial.predictor.method specifies how predictions of the outcome are estimated in two regressions and contrast regression. Flexible models can be used such as GBM (“boosting”), random forests (“randomForest”) or logistic regression (“logistic”). We chose “logistic” because it is relatively faster than boosting methods and random forest.

  • followup.time specifies the maximum follow-up time in the data. We set it default as NULL, which indicates unknown potential censoring time.

  • tau0 is the horizon for RMTL, chosen as described above; assess follow-up support near this horizon in both treatment groups.

  • higher.y was set to TRUE because relapse is a negative event and longer time to first relapse is more desirable in our example. Hence, we are telling the function that subgroups of high responders to drug1 vs drug0 should have later onset of the first relapse. For a positive event such as discharge, a shorter time may instead be preferable, so higher.y = FALSE may be appropriate. It is important for this argument to match with the nature of y outcome because it will affect how the subgroups are defined by the CATE scores and the performance metrics.

  • surv.min truncates the censoring probability estimated from the IPCW model with a lower limit to prevent extremely small censoring probabilities. It is recommended to choose a small positive value close to 0. We chose 0.025 in the example, which corresponds to the default value.

  • We performed 5 CV iterations by specifying cv.n = 5. Typically, more CV iterations are desirable although associated with longer computational times.

  • We set a random seed seed = 999 to reproduce the results.

  • We avoided generating the boosting performance plots by specifying plot.gbmperf = FALSE.

  • When verbose = 1, progress messages are printed in the R console but errors and warnings are not printed. The current CV iteration is printed, followed by the steps of the CV procedure (splitting the data, training the models, validating the models). A timestamp and a progress bar are also displayed upon completion of a CV iteration. If contrastReg was selected as one of the methods in score.method, an additional line of output message will indicate whether the algorithm has converged.

There are many other non-mandatory arguments that catecv() can accept. Please see the Customizing CATE models and validation vignette for more examples and the Function description Function description for details. If you run into errors or warnings with your data, it might be helpful to go over the descriptions to see if you need to alter the default values. In this toy example, we keep the default values of the remaining arguments.

We reuse the tau0 calculated above so that validation estimates RMTL over the same horizon as the average treatment effect example.

output_catecv <- catecv(response = "survival",
                        data = survival_data,
                        score.method = c("randomForest", "contrastReg"),
                        cate.model = survival::Surv(y, d) ~ age + female +
                                     previous_cost + previous_number_relapses,
                        ps.model = trt ~ age + previous_treatment,
                        initial.predictor.method = "logistic",
                        followup.time = NULL,
                        tau0 = tau0,
                        higher.y = TRUE,
                        surv.min = 0.025,
                        prop.cutoff = seq(0.6, 1, length = 5),
                        prop.multi = c(0, 0.5, 0.6, 1),
                        cv.n = 5,
                        seed = 999,
                        plot.gbmperf = FALSE,
                        verbose = 1)
#> Warning in data.preproc.surv(fun = "crossv", cate.model = cate.model, ps.model = ps.model, : Variable trt was recoded to 0/1 with drug0->0 and drug1->1.
#>   |                                                                              |                                                                      |   0%
#> cv = 1

Inspect validation results

The output of catecv() is an object of class “precmed” and here we named it output_catecv. It carries the relevant information to use in the next step of the workflow which selects the method (among those specified in the argument score.method) capturing the highest level of treatment effect heterogeneity. The output, which is described below, will be used in the functions abc(), plot() and boxplot().

For each method specified in the argument score.method, the following 3 groups of outputs are generated: high, low and group. We use the results from randomForest as an example.

Nested subgroups of high responders

This output stores the ATEs - the ratio of RMTL between drug1 vs drug0 in this example - in nested subgroups of patients of high responders to drug 1 in the training ($ate.est.train.high.cv) and validation ($ate.est.valid.high.cv) sets across all CV iterations. When higher.y = TRUE for survival outcomes, which is the case in this example, lower CATE scores correspond to high responders to drug1. When higher.y = FALSE for survival outcomes, higher CATE scores correspond to high responders to drug1. Note that this is different for count outcomes. The direction of CATE scores depends on both higher.y and outcome type.

output_catecv$ate.randomForest$ate.est.train.high.cv
#>               cv1       cv2       cv3       cv4       cv5
#> prop0.6 0.3963633 0.3754889 0.4010173 0.3997561 0.3641983
#> prop0.7 0.4540380 0.4645004 0.4527744 0.4607592 0.4249463
#> prop0.8 0.5178353 0.5463682 0.5448044 0.5484527 0.5157562
#> prop0.9 0.6104817 0.6183804 0.6350983 0.6435192 0.6237003
#> prop1   0.7319446 0.7402708 0.7466061 0.7498346 0.7381476
output_catecv$ate.randomForest$ate.est.valid.high.cv
#>               cv1       cv2       cv3       cv4       cv5
#> prop0.6 0.6378214 0.6492408 0.6459395 0.6165065 0.6346245
#> prop0.7 0.6544669 0.6751040 0.6365238 0.5930391 0.6517549
#> prop0.8 0.6652150 0.6857915 0.7103078 0.6080198 0.6806425
#> prop0.9 0.7175058 0.7202874 0.7091834 0.6386998 0.7083482
#> prop1   0.7399158 0.7288633 0.6839708 0.6668245 0.7141957

The output is a matrix with columns corresponding to the CV iterations, labeled from 1 to cv.n, and rows corresponding to nested subgroups. The nested subgroups of patients are defined by the argument prop.cutoff. Here, we use seq(0.6, 1, length = 5) which defines nested subgroups with the 60%, 70%, 80%, 90% and 100% lowest (highest if higher.y = FALSE) CATE scores estimated by random forest. The rows in the output are labeled to reflect the user-specified proportions used to build the subgroups.

For example, in the training set and in the 4th CV iteration (4th column labeled “cv4”), the subgroup defined with the 80% lowest CATE scores (3rd row labeled “prop0.8”) has an estimated RMTL ratio of 0.548. In contrast, the subgroup defined with all patients (last row labeled “prop1”) in the 4th CV iteration has an estimated RMTL ratio of 0.75.

Nested subgroups of low responders

This output stores the ATEs in nested subgroups of low responders to drug1 in the training ($ate.est.train.low.cv) and validation ($ate.est.valid.low.cv) sets across all CV iterations. When higher.y = TRUE for survival outcomes, higher CATE scores correspond to low responders to drug1. When higher.y = FALSE for survival outcomes, lower CATE scores correspond to low responders to drug1. Again, this is different for count outcomes. The direction of CATE scores depends on both higher.y and outcome type.

output_catecv$ate.randomForest$ate.est.train.low.cv
#>              cv1      cv2      cv3      cv4      cv5
#> prop0.4 1.637613 1.881854 1.727037 1.730834 1.930266
#> prop0.3 2.020644 2.264075 2.158462 2.122557 2.409761
#> prop0.2 2.703428 2.995450 2.710862 2.867130 3.191465
#> prop0.1 4.200552 6.760649 4.659918 3.994933 4.522125

The outputs are also matrices with columns corresponding to the CV iterations and rows corresponding to nested subgroups.

The output for the low responders brings additional information to the user. It gives the ATEs in the complement of each nested subgroup of high responders. For example, the complement of the subgroup of high responders defined as patients with the 60% lowest (highest if higher.y = FALSE) estimated CATE scores is the subgroup of low responders defined as patients with the 40% highest (lowest if higher.y = FALSE) estimated CATE scores, labeled as “prop0.4”. In the training set and in the first CV iterations, the estimated RMTL ratio is 0.396 in the 60% high responders to drug 1 and 1.638 in the 40% low responders.

Mutually exclusive subgroups

This output stores the ATEs in mutually exclusive multi-category subgroups of patients in the training ($ate.est.train.group.cv) and validation ($ate.est.valid.group.cv) sets across all CV iterations.

output_catecv$ate.randomForest$ate.est.train.group.cv
#>               cv1       cv2       cv3       cv4       cv5
#> prop0.5 1.4985779 1.6532249 1.5202768 1.5581822 1.5736821
#> prop0.6 0.7923347 0.6210234 0.8840708 0.6910445 0.5844207
#> prop1   0.2119696 0.2241247 0.2427091 0.2494675 0.2504984
output_catecv$ate.randomForest$ate.est.valid.group.cv
#>               cv1       cv2       cv3       cv4       cv5
#> prop0.5 0.9028651 0.7961139 0.7710531 0.7887313 0.8056517
#> prop0.6 0.6403685 0.3654429 0.4068363 0.4349393 0.6160842
#> prop1   0.6419662 0.6668727 0.6936596 0.6092037 0.6000368

The output is a matrix with columns corresponding to the CV iterations and rows corresponding to the mutually exclusive subgroups. The previous 2 outputs only focus on binary subgroups (high or low responders). Here, the mutually exclusive subgroups can be more than 2 and are defined by the argument prop.multi. We use c(0, 0.5, 0.6, 1) which defines 3 subgroups of patients with the 50% lowest, 10% middle and 40% highest estimated CATE scores when higher.y = TRUE (as in this example), or with the 40% highest, 10% middle and 50% lowest estimated CATE scores when higher.y = FALSE. Taking the first column as an example, the first CV iteration calculated 1.499 as the RMTL ratio for the subgroup with the 50% lowest estimated CATE scores, 0.792 as the RMTL ratio for the subgroup with the middle 10% estimated CATE scores, and 0.212 as the RMTL ratio for the subgroup with the 40% highest estimated CATE scores.

Inspect errors and warnings

Subgroup estimates can be missing or unstable, for example when a subgroup has few patients or observed events. The catecv() output records errors and warnings for each method, subgroup and iteration. The following code checks the first iteration for low-responder subgroups using the random forest method:

output_catecv$`errors/warnings`$randomForest$est.train.low.cv$cv1
#> NULL
output_catecv$`errors/warnings`$randomForest$est.valid.low.cv$cv1
#> NULL

For mutually exclusive subgroups, inspect output_catecv$`errors/warnings`$randomForest$est.train.group.cv. Review any convergence warnings and interpret affected estimates with caution.

Compare scoring methods using the ABC statistic

The ABC statistic is calculated by abc() for each scoring method specified in catecv() and for each of the cv.n CV iterations using the output object output_catecv from catecv(). The ABC corresponds to the area between the curve formed by the ATEs in subgroups of high responders in the validation set (e.g., output_catecv$ate.randomForest$ate.est.valid.high.cv for random forest) and the horizontal line representing the ATE in the validation set. A higher ABC indicates greater separation in the expected direction in this example. Chapter 20 discusses this responder diagnostic (Jiang et al. 2026).

output_abc <- abc(output_catecv)
output_abc
#>                     cv1        cv2         cv3        cv4        cv5
#> randomForest 0.03287103 0.01887424 0.002458051 0.02759943 0.01929065
#> contrastReg  0.04410396 0.03072848 0.003506700 0.03757073 0.01844972

The output is a matrix with columns corresponding to the CV iterations and rows corresponding to the scoring methods specified in score.method. For example, random forest in CV iteration 1 has an ABC of 0.033, in the first CV iteration; compare it with the other scoring methods rather than relying on a single split. The user can combine the ABC for each method across iterations:

average_abc <- apply(output_abc, 1, mean)
average_abc
#> randomForest  contrastReg 
#>   0.02021868   0.02687192

In this example, random forest also offers the best overall performance because it has the highest average ABC, followed closely by contrast regression.

Assess responder discrimination with validation curves

Chapter 20 discusses validation curves, ABC statistics, and their interpretation as responder diagnostics (Jiang et al. 2026). These summaries assess how well a score ranks patients by treatment benefit; they do not, by themselves, establish calibration of the predicted CATEs or the clinical value of a treatment rule (Thao et al. 2026).

The ATEs of nested subgroups of high responders to drug1 (e.g., output_catecv$ate.randomForest$ate.est.train.high.cv and output_catecv$ate.randomForest$ate.est.valid.high.cv for random forest) can be visualized as a side-by-side line plot, with training results on the left and validation results on the right. The x-axis is determined by prop.cutoff and the y-axis is the estimated ATEs averaged over cv.n CV iterations as specified by cv.i = NULL (default). The estimated ATE is expressed as a RMTL ratio of drug1 versus drug0 for our toy example. By default, the function retrieves the name of the treatment variable (trt) and the original labels (drug0 and drug1) to specify a meaningful y-axis label. Otherwise, it is possible to customize the y-axis label via the ylab, for example, by specifying ylab = “RMTL ratio of drug1 vs drug0 in each subgroup”.

Separation between the validation curve and the overall ATE can indicate that the score ranks patients by treatment benefit. Because higher.y = TRUE in this example, a useful ranking would tend to produce lower RMTL ratios on the left, increasing toward the overall ratio as the subgroup expands (see Validation curves and the ABC statistics). The validation curves and ABC can help compare methods, but selection on these same results warrants an independent assessment.

plot(output_catecv)

The random forest shows stronger subgroup separation in training than in validation, consistent with possible overfitting. Its validation curve nevertheless rises toward the overall ratio as the selected subgroup expands. Contrast regression shows more similar training and validation curves, with a lower validation ratio for the selected subgroup than for the overall group. Both methods show some validation separation in the expected direction, but the plot does not show uncertainty and does not establish that either method will perform well in new patients. An independent evaluation is needed before drawing firm conclusions.

The dashed gray line is the overall treatment ratio in the corresponding training or validation sets, averaged across iterations. The curves meet it at a subgroup size of 100% because that subgroup includes everyone in each respective set.

To inspect a single cross-validation iteration instead of the average, set cv.i in plot(); for example, cv.i = 2 selects the second iteration. You can use combine = "median" to show the median across iterations instead of the default mean.

To compare both measures across the nested subgroups, use measure = c("rmtl", "cumulative_hr"). The panels show the RMTL ratio and the cumulative hazard ratio separately; the latter summarizes cumulative hazards up to tau0 and is not an instantaneous Cox HR. ABC is shown only for the RMTL plot above.

plot(output_catecv, measure = c("rmtl", "cumulative_hr"))

In each panel, the dashed line is the overall ratio for that measure in the corresponding training or validation sets, averaged across iterations. It is a reference for comparing the score-defined subgroups, not a line of no treatment effect. Objects saved before cumulative hazard ratios were added need to be refitted to plot them.

Compare treatment effects across responder subgroups

Unlike the nested groups in validation curves, these subgroups are mutually exclusive within each iteration. The boxes summarize variation in subgroup estimates across validation iterations. Chapter 20 compares these responder diagnostics (Jiang et al. 2026).

The ATEs of multi-category subgroups that are mutually exclusive can be visualized as box plots, with 1 box plot for each scoring method. Only validation results are visualized here. The x-axis is determined by prop.multi and the y-axis is the estimated ATEs in each subgroup. We specify the ylab argument accordingly. The subgroups correspond to each row of the ate.est.valid.group.cv result in output_catecv, so in this example the subgroups are patient with the 50% lowest (0-50%), middle 10% (50-60%), and highest 40% (60-100%) estimated CATE scores. Notice that the groups do not have to be equally spaced in terms of percentiles. The box plot shows the distribution of the ATEs over all cv.n CV iterations, instead of a summary statistics like mean or median in plot().

boxplot(output_catecv,
        ylab = "RMTL ratio of drug1 vs drug0 in each subgroup")

Cumulative hazard ratios can also be shown for the mutually exclusive subgroups:

boxplot(output_catecv, measure = "cumulative_hr")

The box plots compare estimated RMTL ratios across mutually exclusive score-based subgroups for random forest and contrast regression. Read them alongside the validation curves and ABC statistics to assess subgroup separation and variation across CV iterations. Note that the y-axis can have different scales for different scoring methods.



So far we provided 3 different metrics to summarize, visualize, and evaluate the catecv() outputs. The user is encouraged to choose their own way of data wrangling that fits to their particular situation.
